I'd never really understood the desire to play a video game about doing work. Car Mechanic Simulator was a fun gimmick, but Farming Simulator? That just sounds ridiculous... and it is.

This game is ridiculously relaxing, rewarding, and enjoyable. There's a lot more than just "farming" too. There's the aspect of building a farm, laying out where buildings will go, organizing tractors, trucks, and tools. There's the whole financial strategy part too; do i buy this tractor, lease it, or continue to use the old basic piece of junk for another harvest or two, and should i plant corn and turn it into silage, or plant soybeans for profit, maybe plant oat and bale the straw afterwards? It's just crazy how much honestly goes on in a simple simulator. And with mods, this game can even become a farm manager game as you send workers out to plow, cultivate, harvest, transport crop, etc.

I love it though. I can work all day, getting stressed and frustrated, but then come home and relax as I just let the tractor drive lines up and down a field planting, or use a harvester to collect crops, and it's just so damn easy to get lost in.

I know a lot of people look at Farming Sim and laugh, but this is honestly one of the best games I've put my time into. I mean, 568 hrs at this point in time... It's worth every penny.

After playing for just a couple hours I already couldn't even imagine going back to FS17. 80 hours later, farming still feels better than it ever did before. Good job Giants :D

Almost every single aspect of the game has been improved from FS17 in some way. Most notably:

- item handling: Moving things by hand is no longer frustrating! Things no longer fly out of your hand whenever you touch anything, no Herculean strength to flip tractors with a piece of wood and able to rotate items in-hand. Looking forward to conventional balers at this point.

- vehicle handling: greatly improved, steering feels much more realistic (using keyboard), you can feel you're driving a several ton piece of machinery, suspension and ground response better than ever

- vehicle maintenance: vehicles no longer have daily maintenance fee, instead they have wear and tear that you have to fix for a small fee (similar to what Seasons mod did in FS17), resulting in massive decrease in passive running cost for the farm (idle vehicles don't cost you)

- land management: you no longer own entire map except the fields, land/field expansion feels more natural with having to buy the land. Buy a forest, cut down the trees and turn it into farmland!

- buildings: finally able to build up your own farm other than just adding a couple sheds, although placing stuff on anything but a very flat ground can cause issues. Upcoming terraforming feature will fix that, potentially. Also choice of buildings in base game is limited, but I'm sure modding community fill flood the game with dozens of new items soon.

- field management: new lime and weeds mechanics, greatly expanding on the "fertilize 3 times" approach from FS17, more stuff to do between sowing and harvesting phases

- new stuff: cotton, horses, sugarcane (for those without FS17 platinum). All with their own mechanics/machinery. More variety of stuff to do, even if cotton is pretty bad profit compared to other crops.

- contracts: complete overhaul of missions, much less clunky although somewhat buggy at the moment (weeds will overtake NPC fields permanently)

- animals: chickens are finally not useless, as eggs will spawn in boxes without having to collect them manually. Placeable animal pens require higher initial investment in livestock, similar to buying fields for arable farms. 

- shop: better separation of vehicles and implements into categories, full 3D preview of machinery and its configuration ("Does this tractor look silly with narrow tires and painted pink? Did that trailer have a hitch on the back or not? I'll just look and see!")

- graphics: not a massive leap forward but pretty good upgrade overall, game feels to be running smoother than FS17 too. Big improvements in lighting and atmospheric visuals, you can easily see the difference in the overall image and feel of the game. Beautiful sunsets and night lights :)

- audio: a lot of good enviromental sounds, engine sounds stand out much more than in FS17

- interface: new interface look, much cleaner, more readable and compact


Stuff that did not improve (or marginally):
- AI Workers: Almost as derpy as always :D, seem to miss less parts of a field on angled edges though
- Logging: while the new chainsaw animation is good, it seems 'aiming' the cuts is less intuitive, pieces of wood can still get glitched after cutting (weird collision box and mass) and still missing any sound when a massive tree falls down. Need that satisfying 'creeeeeak-THUD'

While the game sure has some issues currently, none are too serious or game-breaking (as far as I've encoutered).

Lets get this out of the way. I've been playing FS since 2013. Its one of my favorite game franchises. But it seems that after FS13, Giants has never really gave the games a big improvement and supposedly this was supposed to be that big improvement. The graphics are....okay. But I'll get into that later.

Pros:
- Lots of Brands! Great variety (although they insist on keeping the EU SMV warning signs so when you go to an American map it breaks my immersion)
- Purchasing land is a lot more realistic to me and more enjoyable.
- Finally, after years and years of waiting, we have a store where you can see what you're buying.
Cons:
- Hardly any real new improvements. Graphics are virtually the same as FS17 but with a few minor changes.
- Physics, they're laughable. Hit the accelerator in a John Deere 6155M and suddenly immediately you're going warp speed. Steering is still awful and gives no feedback, suspension on vehicles is stiffer than stiff. For a simulator series thats been going on for 10+ years, this is really bad considering I can boot up FS13 and get virtually the same experience.
- Horsepower? HA! That's irrelevant in FS19, doesn't matter what Harvester you get, you are stuck at the speed the game tells you to go.
- The game is optimized TERRIBLY, that reason alone is why I REALLY recommend to stick with one of the older games like FS15 or 17. Its jittery, barely runs at points if you look at more than one piece of equipment. For a game that graphically isn't much better than 17, its terribly thirsty for a really beefy system, and I can run games such as BO4 and GTA V at a solid 60FPS AT LEAST.
- Everything drives like a arcade racer. 
- AI workers are still, not useless, but about as close to useless as you can get. Because as long as you keep an eye on them and fix their mistakes they make (like not finishing the edges of a field) you should be fine. But that's just a band-aid for poor design.

Unfortunately, it seems Giants is more interested in adding things like....dogs? To the game instead of fixing existing issues. There's more cons that I haven't bothered to list since I believe they've already been so well documented to the point I think it should be easy to look them up. Its a shame, look at a game like Halo CE and 9 years later in Halo Reach, you can see major graphical improvements. Every iteration of FS doesn't feel like something I'd pay $30 for again but more so a $10 update to a previous game. Lets be honest, everything new in FS19 isn't anything that couldn't have been added to FS17 or FS15, and that's becoming a big problem with this series. I still can have fun with it, but I'm very underwhelmed.

Ah, Farming Simulator. It all started that one night, browsing the Steam store for games on sale, and I stumbled upon FS19, 20% off. And I chuckled a bit, thinking 'hah, that would have been funny. Sitting here, pretending to be farming!'
I searched up some streams on Twitch, wanting to see how people actually played the game, and I watched a guy filling a silage clamp for 45 minutes, talking about his day.
How I went from that, to purchasing the game - I don't know. But here we are, over 300 in-game hours later and not feeling a natural stopping point. I've purchased a complete setup - steering wheel, pedals, two joysticks and to top it off - a newly revived YouTube channel where I post my gameplay. I'm waist deep in this game, and I regret not trying it sooner. It's an addicting game, with a lot of different ways of playing it.

I would highly recommend this game to people, and that's something you will too if you start playing. Make sure you have loving and understanding people around you if you plan on purchasing this game - because you'll find a sudden need to tell people around you about farming.

The good:
Lots of brands.
They added a store where you can see the equipment before buying it.

The bad:
The gameplay has not changed much from the original 2009 edition, less so from the 2017 version.
Many vehicles have defects in their models, many unacceptable considering they have licences (Valtra N series has both electronic and mechanical controls, since its a reused model of FS17 that was modified).
Maps have horrible defects not present in older Farming Simulators, for example, rail track crossings actually sit over the road instead of in it.

The game calls itself a simulator despite having all models of reduced weight and filtypes that most of the time weight less than half of their actual weight, for example 1000L of water weight less than 600kg.

Game does not posses gearboxes as promised, this combined with the reduced weight of vehicles makes tractors handle like Go-Carts (mods have been built in the past for this, ignored by Giants).

Zero crop simulation other than the amount of times fertilizer is applied and weed control (which happens all the time no matter what). Weather does not affect crops, there is no growing seasons so you can seed and harvest crops at the same time, eliminating any sense of order in the game. "Compaction" is incorrectly fixed by using ploughs, a tool well known to generate compaction (both by reducing the soil structure and the building of plough pans).

Horsepower of any type of harvester does not matter, you will still harvest at the same speed no matter if you combine has 200hp or 500hp and no matter the size of the header. Same with balers.
In any type of work, the only limiting factor is speed, not throughput, not pulling force. Mods simulating this have been build in the past multiple times, but Giants keeps ignoring them.

Ai workers are still not smart enough to drive on the road or do anything other than field work.
Ai drivers still miss spots, get caught on trees, stop unexpectedly, turn in the wrong direction, etcetera.

Manure or any product put on fields can't be cultivated over if the field has already been cultivated.
Dedicated no till drills still remove every residue on the soil.

Graphics;
The ambient in general looks oversaturated with light.
Far away mountains look worse than a 2005 game.
Metal textures lack roughness and many look like base colours in sunlight.
They couldn't even fix the problem of rain falling through roofs of buildings and vehicles, it basically rains inside the cab.
Wipers are just plain moving sticks, there is zero interaction of rain with windshields (a feature present in basically any car or truck simulator in the market a few years ago).
Crops look very spaced, nowhere near the density of a real crop. Same with grass.

A friend of mine who sells Ponsse machinery laughed at the way the Buffalo handles logs, IRL the machine can pick and load multiple logs in one grab with utter precision and force. In game the machine can barely grab one log, and the log tends to slide and glitch out of the machine, the claw has no force at all.
At the end forestry machinery ends up being frustrating and unrewarding to play correctly.


I could keep on going, however all you need to know is this is not a simulator, and don't expect nice graphics anyways.
All of this would maybe be acceptable if this was the third or fourth iteration of the game, however its the seventh, not considering the platinium/gold editions.

I do love this game, I had fun playing with friends too and I will continue to play it. Relaxing game overall. BUT THE TRUTH IS, THERE ARE MANY SIDES MAKE ME FEEL LIKE I'M PLAYING AN ''UNFINISHED'' BEAUTIFUL GAME. Here is my opinion after 270 hours of gameplay both single and multiplayer. Theseare STRONGLY POSITIVE and STRONGLY NEGATIVE SIDES:

+ Raising livestock is very realistic and enjoyable that you have to use different combinations of food, hay, grass etc. for them. Keep them clean, fed and give them clean water which will feel like doing the real thing... 

+ You can use livestock byproducts like slurry and manure in your fields. Fields need plowing, lime, fertilizers etc. and these needs can be turned on/off. There are different kinds of crops you can grow, prices change day by day and some plants take longer to grow. 

+ Many very realistic farming equipments and mechanics. Forestry, husbandry and plantation are all enjoyable and beautiful...

+ Plenty of nice mods you will absolutely love trying! 

+ Multiplayer has no problems like disconnections, big time bugs, mod problems etc. Multiplayer works very good and solid! You can use mods in multiplayer without any problems too if you all have the same mods installed which is a GREAT THING!

- Game actually could be named ''BABYSITTING YOUR STUPID ASS USELESS AF HELPERS SIMULATOR'' because if you really want to get too big in this game you'll need helpers. BUT Helper AI is TERRIBLE! They are so stupid in that they can NOT BE CALLED ''artificial intelligence'' because I'm pretty sure there actually is NO intelligence in those helpers. So you don't have an option like ''Let me hire workers to sow and fertilize my lands meanwhile I feed my cows, pigs and sheep and sell my products! Because your workers will do things wrong and YOU HAVE TO CORRECT THOSE HUGE MISTAKES THEY MAKE! The truth is they can't even get the work perfectly done with vanilla lands or the most perfectly shaped lands a monkey could do IRL... (I'll upload screenshots of how terrible and useless they exactly are)

- Driving mechanics are a bit bad for a game like this which has so many different type of vehicles. Every type of vehicle be it a truck, a car, a harvester, a tractor feels like you're driving a 1945 model old ass tractor. Just don't expect perfected drive mechanics... 

- Physics are BAD! Your big ass American type truck weighing 5 tons with 110 tons of soybeans loaded CAN FLY LIKE A LITTLE BIRD in the air. Not a big deal for me as physics are not the first thing I look for in this game... 

I'll give it 7/10 and recommend FOR THE SAKE OF great multiplayer, very realistic livestock, forestry, mod system and  in game market price system. But I say it again FS19 AI is the worst I've seen that I really want to hug and apologize to PD2/L4D2 bots and scripted Skyrim NPC's for calling them stupid before. I bought Farming Simulator 19 on a whim during a midweek sale; I wanted a relaxing simulator and there were few games in my vast library that I knew would fit the criteria. I have little prior experience with farming sims; I played Farming Simulator 13 for around twenty hours, became frustrated with its lack of direction, and ended up dumping it because I had a technical issue that the developers didn't help with on the forum. Thus, I was a little leery of supporting this one.

78 hours of gametime later, I'm in love. Farming Simulator 19 offers you many tutorials and aids to help newcomers learn how to grow crops (of which there are different types of harvesters, sometimes extra steps, etc.) and raise animals. Sometimes it still shows lack of direction--I spent five hours on a starter map looking for the next step in the tutorial. The game wouldn't let me freeplay until finishing it, but it was missing. So I restarted on a freeplay map and figured out everything from scratch. Still, this wasn't overly stressful; the game advances at a relaxing pace to where you have plenty of time to prepare for the next venture (new field, new equipment, new crop/animal, etc.) and research its requirements online. Trial and error is to be expected. Early on, I almost ran out of money because a new field I bought already had sugar beets planted, so I decided to lease all corresponding equipment to harvest it since I couldn't afford to buy it. Leasing everything cost me $23K when the harvest granted $26K in profit. Thankfully all was well, but had I any idea how complicated it would be beforehand, I would have waited for the AI to harvest it before purchasing the lot. The game doesn't warn you when you're about to make stupid decisions, so with each major purchase, you need to do a lot of research!

In fact, Farming Simulator 19 [i]never[/i] tells you what to do. It is a true simulation that allows you every freedom. Everything is customizable, even a lot of crucial game options. You can choose whether or not your equipment gets visibly dirty, weeds grow with every harvest, lime and/or periodic plowing is required to maintain yield, and you can even quicken or slow down time. This last point is my favorite because it allows you to play the game at any pace you want, from where 24 hours passes in 12 minutes (120x speed) to where it's based on real-time, so each in-game minute is one real-life minute. I'd often play in real-time until all my chores on my land were done, then do missions from other farmers to make money until there were no more jobs I wanted to do (Hint: harvesting jobs make the best profit, for you get the job money and a percentage of the harvest income). Then, "fast forward" until other fields develop, do more missions, etc. In this way, you can manipulate the world to where you can maximize the amount of money you make in a day to further protect you from bankruptcy. Because you can hire helpers to do many jobs for you, you can focus on doing those you like best (say, harvesting) while getting the AI to do the others. All of these jobs can be happening simultaneously. As long as you have the equipment and time, you can be working the land all over the map at once with aid from workers.

I grew up on a ranch, and out of all the pets I've ever had (more than two dozen species), chickens were by far the most fun. Farming Simulator 19 is one of the few games that allows me to experience just a bit of that joy as an adult living in the suburbs, and I'm grateful to it. You can also raise horses, sheep, cows, and pigs, though you can only name horses. I would have loved the option to name all animals to give it a more personal touch. Additionally, I hope in the future Giants Software considers building upon the helper system. It's great to have helpers, but they don't have names and aren't hired for good. I think it'd be nice for Farming Simulator to go the way of SCS Software's Truck Simulator series (Euro and American), to where you could hire and manage actual employees, even assigning certain jobs for them to do automatically. The only other request I'd have is for more crops and corresponding equipment. I'd love to tend to orchards or even just grow something more exciting than the roster of grains (and few others like potatoes, sugar beets).

In summary, Farming Simulator 19 is a perfect gateway into farming sims for players looking to start. You can play your way: actively, by tending to every task yourself and fast-forwarding through growth phases, or passively, by assigning AI to tasks and slowing time down to a crawl. If you love tending to and building a business in a relaxing atmosphere, Farming Simulator 19 is one of the few games that captures that unique feeling. This game sits next to those in the Truck Simulator franchise as one of my go-to relaxing simulators. I look forward to seeing Giants Software continue to innovate and grow the series.

[b]At the end of the day, this is a case of 'too little too late'.[/b]

[i]Farming Simulator 19[/i] offers a good bit of fun and content - but it still suffers from some fundamental design problems that are painful to see still persisting in the latest edition. These issues could certainly be overlooked a decade ago, but now after six or so versions of the game - a lot of it becomes unexcusable. For instance, how can any self-proclaimed farming simulator not have seasons this far into the franchise? Seasons are so critical to farming that I can't begin to understand why they are not in the base game at this point. Also, the core mechanic is interacting with fields, so why don't we have a more dynamic tire and soil interaction? This is basic stuff. I could go on. This simulator still largely boils down to 'painting' fields.

[b]While some will have you think [i]Giants Software[/i] has the market cornered - mark my words - all it will take is a small indie team with a few bucks and an open mind to topple this series.[/b] It's not that difficult of a game to get right, and it's only a matter of time. Let me explain why I say this. For those that aren't familiar with the community, what you need to know is that it has a strong [i]'old guard'[/i] attitude. While the community is mostly nice, long standing members (including the developers) are largely unwilling to accept or consider new ideas. This is the core problem. This series may be the best you can get right now in the farming simulation genre, but it leaves a lot to be desired (compared to, say, [i]American Truck Simulator[/i] which feels darned near perfect for that genre). 

[b]Pros:[/b]
+It's a remarkably fun time sink.
+There is a lot of content, and mods are icing on the cake.
+The multiplayer aspect adds a lot.
+For the most part, it's all quite beautiful.

[b]Meh:[/b]
=I'm the last person to talk about graphics, but these are a bit of a letdown. It still feels a bit dated or something (particularly the 2D soil).
=The character creator is sort of a tease. Yes, thank you for adding it in, but it is the absolute bare-minimum it could be. What would it take to simply expand on it?

[b]Cons:[/b]
-The series as a whole needs to evolve at a much faster rate.

-Mouse sensitivity is horribly low even at the maximum of 200%. Who could playtest this for more than 20 minutes and not realize this?
-Why does the American map look so trashy? This is a big complaint from me, because it was clearly a deliberate design choice. Sure, I've witnessed American farmland that looks like this - but I've also seen plenty of much less rundown farmland in America. Why not make it a bit more pleasant. -For being a 'simulator', there actually isn't all that much content that reflects this. For example, you can 'tab' teleport between vehicles, break signs in the town with impunity (how about a small monetary fine?), and 'paint' fields haphazardly with no penalty, among other things. 

[b]If you haven't played any of the [i]Farming Simulator[/i] titles and are interested - go for it.[/b] WIth that being said, I am not hopeful that this series is going to ever innovate beyond what we essentially already have in front of us.

I have over 150 hours clocked up in FS17, which was a game I found to be highly addictive. So I thought I was on to a winner when I bought FS19.

Unfortunately not. Don't get me wrong. This is just as addictive as it's predecessor, but..... that's about it. I Only started playing a couple of days ago, and having clocked 10+ hours now, I still haven't really noticed any improvements or advantages over FS17. One of the marketing claims was a massive graphical improvement. Well... where is it? All i've noticed is a horrible and somewhat exaggerated orange peel effect on vehicle bodywork. I haven't seen anything else which has been graphically improved.

The main things that annoyed me in FS17 are still present in FS19:

- Helpers still cannot identify a separation between fields. So if you set up one worker to plow a field, keep an eye on them, otherwise you could be losing an entire neighbouring field of crops as well!
- Helpers still cannot finish a task if the field they are working in is not square/rectangular. I've already had messages popping up saying "Helper X has completed their task" when in fact half of the field has been missed, because it curves one way or the other.

The beacons all appear to have broken lenses. The silver colour of the rotating reflector is always visible, as if a piece of the lens is missing.

The controls are a bit messed up compared with FS17. I have assigned all the same controls between the two games. But in FS19, when I press the button assigned to Rear Work Lights, I get the Pause Menu. On foot, if I walk forward, the chainsaw appears. I ended up having to sell it to solve that problem.

There are various little issues like this which you really wouldn't expect to find in a game which claims to have been massively overhauled and refined since the previous version.


Maybe I just haven't put enough time into the game yet, but the fact the helper issues are still present is incredibly frustrating. Having to go round after them to correct their mistakes or finish the job they were meant to do (just as I had to in FS17), defeats the object of hiring them at all.

I'll continue to play, since it is, in essence, still very addictive. It's just a shame that it's really a re-badged version of FS17.

If I find a good enough reason to change my opinion, I will update this review accordingly. But for now, I remain unimpressed.

I've been a "fan" of the farming sim genre for a while now. I got really hooked on Farm Simulator 2013 -- I probably put 200 hours into that game, which was way more than I anticipated.  I tried again with '14, '15, '17 and now '19 but so far nothing has recaptured that feel for me yet. 

I'm not even into the game that far yet, but I can recognize they've added a bunch of options and made it much more customizable. For one thing, you have a lot of options for crops to raise.  Back in '13 it was wheat, barley, canola, corn, potatos, and beets, and oh yeah, you could just let the fields grow grass and cut that for hay bales.  This game has a lot more options for crops -- 13 different crops including grain, root crops (potatoes etc), cotton, sugarcane, and sunflowers.

There's also a lumber side-gig you can do where you chop trees down (with machinery) to sell to a lumber yard.  I don't know if that's really going to be something I'll want to do since to me the idea of waiting for a tree to grow so I can cut it down and sell it for profit sounds like a boring job.  If you're talking about a forest then it's different.

The types of animals you can have has also increased from just "Chickens, sheep, and cows" in '13 to chickens, cows, horses, pigs, and sheep, as well as additions to you can do with them.  Before it was just eggs, milk and wool... oh and manure for slurry/fertilizing.   I don't yet know if this is a good change, and as I figure it out I'll edit this review. 

Of course they've added a bunch of different machinery types, so you can feel all manly driving a multitude of different tractors and other vehicles, but they also gave you options for buying vs leasing (which is actually more like renting).  If there's a vehicle you only need rarely, you could just lease it and then return it when you're done instead of spending the large amount of cash for something you barely use.

Another change is that they've added the ability to buy and place your own farmhouse.  In the original game you had one farmhouse with a small nearby field, and then you slowly bought up all the other land plots around you to increase your farm's size.  Now you could potentially buy/build a new house for every field if you wanted. 

There's also mods supported much like every Farm sim game ever (at least as far as I know) and you can play this online with friends.  In fact I'd go as far as to say that playing it online is probably the best way to go, since offline single-player feels like you're the only person in town.  There are AI cars that drive around, but they really don't do anything more than provide scenery and obstacles for you as you drive from point A to point B.

Unlike older games in the series, there's very little online documentation about this game unless you like watching youtube videos that take 26 minutes to get to the point you're wondering about.  I prefer a nice manual or at the bare minimum, a wiki that I can consult for help.  The in-game help is just about useless by telling you almost nothing about each category, so without a wiki or a manual you're going to be running to the steam forums to find the answers.  The really bad thing is that nobody finds out the answers without a lot of trial and error and in some cases, LOTS of errors.  How hard is it to make a dang manual Giants?

The older games also had some kind of extra side-quest type stuff that encouraged you to fully explore the map.  In 2013 there was a bunch of horseshoes littering the countryside (but no horses strangely enough) and if you found enough horseshoes it would trigger an event.  One of the later games (2015 maybe?) had you looking for actual gold bars lying around.  I had an easier time believing that someone might leave horseshoes lying around, but both served the same purpose: find them for an achievement and maybe to trigger some event.  So far as I can tell in 2019 this doesn't happen.   

It was kind of a pointless easter egg hunt in the earlier games so maybe they decided that few people really cared about it and removed it.  I liked it because it gave me a reason to wander around the map on foot while I waited for my crops to grow.   I could easily have just cranked the time compression up to max and then back down to real-time to harvest, but that was equally boring since I just wound up staying there watching the crops grow.  

Overall though, I don't find this game as interesting as the first game I played.  I don't know if that's because I already burned out on the idea of being a video game farmer, or if it's just that the game mechanics are kinda dry and repetitive.  This is a game I'd give a "meh" thumb to if I could.   It's not worth investing hundreds of hours into without friends who are also into the game, but it's not so terrible that I'd warn someone off of it entirely.

I'm starting to think at this point that you'd be better off getting FS 2017 and then modding it up to 2019 standards.  I've had the game crash on me a couple of times out of nowhere (just randomly as far as I can tell. I can't reproduce the error anyway) and I've purchased an item that sells in the store as a planter only to find out it can only be loaded with dry fertilizer).  

My advice would be to try one of the earlier incarnations of this game that are much simpler in scope like Farm Simulator 2013, and if you like that one, you might also want this one for the expanded options.  The thumbs up is basically because I don't hate it...but I haven't really yet come to love it either.  Your mileage may vary.  If you enjoy building your own farm and paying back a loan then maybe you'll find it engaging enough -- That was one of the original aspects of the game that I enjoyed.

I got on board the Farming Simulator series at 17, so I'm not really an old hat at this game series (yet). But for me, thus far, it's  an excellent way to relax and just do something that takes no effort to do. That said, I recognize that there are some shortcomings here, none of which affect the gameplay enough to shift me from a "yes" to a "no" but should be acknowledged:

*FS17 had a map where a player could roll their machines up to dispensers on the farm and have them automatically filled and charged money for the transaction, likely more than it would cost to buy pallets and manually fill the tool. FS19 lacking this option for slightly less involved play, and modders having to add the functionality afterwards, is a slight black mark in my eyes. Obviously most people in this game will want the full experience--get a loader, load the seed/fertilizer/whatever on a pallet fork, dump it into the machine--but if the previous title offers a gameplay option to the player, I feel that the sequel ought not take it away.

*FS17 also had a system by which repeatedly doing jobs for the same farmer visibly accumulated "friendship points" for lack of a better term which translated to better pay and a better price for buying land from that farmer. If FS19 retained this, there's no indication of it. I believe an incentive to build a reputation with the NPCs is another instance of a gameplay feature that a prior had that its direct sequel ought not to have removed.

*Until the player become wealthy enough to be managing many fields at once, there is very little to do other than fill contracts for money. When your field is plowed, cultivated, seeded, fertilized, and limed, all there is to do is stare at it, until the next growing stage, and then until its finished growing. A minor complaint to be sure, but there's a fine line between idle relaxation and boring and early game flirts with it.

*This game oozes real-world machinery out of every pore. There are an enormous number of options for what to drive, what to use to seed, cultivate, plow, spray, fertilize, and so on. The sheer content volume and variety is impressive and appreciated. And most of it, there's no reason to touch except for the fun of it. You have a fast tractor with a front-loader attachment that you can get immediately at the start which can be upgraded to have more horsepower for tools than anything short of the most expensive light tractor. The Khun subsoil cultivator/plow is more cost-effective than buying the two tools separately, and is quite cheap. Buying the most inexpensive fertilizer spreader and a weeder beats everything until you're rich. In essence, especially if you're challenging yourself most of the content may as well not even exist. I list this as a downside, but I fully acknowledge that even if there is a solution, it'd be a headache to figure out so this, like the others, is a very minor complaint.

As of 26 hours in, these are the only things I see that could be downsides to this game. Wtih how small they are, it seems fair to say that this is a truly excellent experience that I heartily recommend. I'm now looking forward to Farming Simulator 21.

I came from FS17 with high expectations, but it rapidly became blatantly obvious that Farming Simulator relies upon the good will and efforts of the modding community. Even with the few mods currently available for FS19, I'm essentially playing a vanilla version of the game. No real physics, no real weather, no seasons. Only a small handful of maps available, to bolster the 2 maps that come with the game. For me, with FS17, it was a way to pass the time, thinking about life as I nurtured my crops, but there was a diverse stockpile of mods to make things slightly more realistic. 

FS19 suffers because the modding community hasn't been able to transfer their FS17 mods to this latest version. And for me, that demonstrates how little Giant/Focus actually do to create a fantastic game. Farming Simulator definitely relies upon the unsung heroes, the people who don't get paid, to create content for a very basic game. It's as though the devs had a meeting and said, "Real mud? Real physics? Real seasons and weather? Nah, we don't have to do that. That's too much like hard work. Let the modders do it for us."

In truth, FS19 has the potential to become a great game (the graphics are slightly improved over FS17, and there's the option to start from scratch and buy tracts of land as you increase the size of your farm), but without the modders, it's not worth getting if you already have FS17. I stopped playing FS17 because I was hoping FS19 would be a vast improvement. It's not.

Will you like this game? Beats me. If you like relaxing, strategy/time management games and get inspired by a seemingly endless array of machinery and other things to strive for, then  you'll probably enjoy the game. But that's not why I'm bothering to write this review. I'm writing this review because the most remarkable thing about this game is how well it works. In a sea of games that struggle to provide what they promise, this game is amazing.

I have 68 mods activated, and the game takes less than 10 seconds to load and start. I have 6 fields, tons of equipment and placeables, co-op partners, half-a-dozen AI workers going at once, etc. and the game has never once dipped below the 60 FPS that I have it set at--and I'm playing on a laptop. I've had the game crash once and that was on a custom map-created by a modder-that conflicted with one of my mods.

Speaking of mods, the modding is incredible. You can install mods directly from the in-game menu, or you can go to their mod-hub website and download them to the mod folder. Super easy. There are so many great mods that it extends the playability by a considerable margin. Many mods are uploaded by the developers themselves, including bonus maps from previous versions of the game and many equipment packs. They could sell these as DLC, but they give them away for free.

I'm just very impressed. Big thumbs up.

The perfect game to chill out. I have not played previous FS games so my opinion is from someone completely new to the series.

At the beginning you'll get stablished with a piece of land, and some cheap tools. You have to sow your fields, make grow and take care of them, and harvest your profits. With the money you'll eventually get new equipment, and so on, and so on.

It's the perfect game to relax after an stressful day of work at the office, or to disconnect your mind of that important project and his deadline. You only have to put some music/radio/podcast, relax and start to enjoy by working on your fields.

This game as odd as it sounds, it's extremely addictive even when it's EXTREMELY repetitive. You will always have an objective on mind (buy that impressive tractor, take care of your chickens or horses, expand your farm with a great piece of land or do the favor that neighbor is asking for). No matter that you have to work on the same fields over and over again. You feel your crops, your farm (and even your dog) as "yours", and you really have to look after them.

As for the simulation aspect of the game, the machinery is beatifully recreated. With all his working parts that you have to operate (deploy, start, etc.), it's really amazing. You will use the flashing lights on the road, the beacon lights when working on the crops,... the attention to detail and the interior cockpits are great. The physics of the fields are amazingly modelled, when your tractor/tool gets in contact, it's really nicely done. You have to watch your speed or some maneuvers if you don't want to roll your tractor and damage everything. The level of simulation is fully customizable, from an easy experience to a more demanding game. I play with an Xbox One pad although I would love to try some special farming sim peripherals. It supports TrackIr which works as expected.

Unfortunately the visuals, depiste great things like the tractors and tools models, the beautiful (germany) map , and some lighting conditions where the game looks stunning, the overall is that it has some flaws like the drawing distance (even expanding it in the developer options menu), some textures that doesn't look that great and the fact that is not well optimized, although I play it at 1440p with all maxed out at +100fps (i7-8700k, rtx2070,32gb ram), it feels that it still needs some polish or maybe a major graphics engine update. Anyway this goes to the background the moment you get hooked to it.

If you like games like ETS2, PC Building or Car Mechanic Simulators, etc. this game is for you. You decide your level of challenge and game pace. You can use it to wind down from more demanding games (after a tense session of flying or racing sims, this game fits perfectly).

If you're interested at all in agriculture or you and a couple friends want to grab a game to mess around with its janky sandbox then this is 100% the game for you. 

Fair warning to everyone looking for an extremely immersive sim, however, as this game is not that. As I mentioned before, the game is quite janky, and while the bugs are amusing (like I managed to do good ol' prop levitation with a bag of seeds to traverse the map faster than any car could drive), they can definitely take you out of the experience if you're hardcore and care about that. Not to mention the farming is not entirely realistic. The game breaks the process down into it's core stages of tilling-nurturing-harvesting but doesn't go in depth into the science behind farming and the methodology each individual real-world farmer chooses to use. There is a partial fix to this, though, as the developers released a free precision farming dlc on their website that adds pH, nitrogen, and soil type factors that us farmers actually have to take into account and the amazing modding community for this game has also introduced seasons and planting time frames. There are still aspects of the industry that go completely unmentioned even with these addons, like irrigation and erosion, but they help add to the realism nonetheless if you so want. 

With all that said, while not being the perfect window into the life of a farmer that people detached from that lifestyle might've wanted to have, the game is relaxing and educational, especially when it comes to equipment brands (even I was introduced to some mighty pieces of equipment I have never heard of before), and I personally love it for when I don't have the chance to be out there on the field myself.

This is a good game. 8/10 for me. Why just 8 points? Well...

- You are the only farmer on a map. There are no NPC vehicles doing farming like you despite there are dozens of fields which you can do contracts for. But you'll never see a NPC harvester doing farming so in the end the world feels somewhat lifeless. 
- Why are there no real NPCs which you can interact with? The pedestrians you see have no collision so you can happily drive through them, nothing happens. You can't talk with them either so they're just here for decoration. Do a car crash, somebody calls the police? Hell no. No damage to your vehicle. Drive against a wall, same. Sucks. Why not doing a bit more GTA style?? 
- The AI helper which you can easily hire for fieldwork is a catastrophe. You basically MUST get the mod "Courseplay". Watch a basic tutorial (e.g. from "The FarmSim Guy"). In 30 minutes you'll get the hang on how to automate your fieldwork. Believe me, this mod is Godsent.
- Raising cattle / animals is very tedious. There is no AI help you can hire which means you have to provide food, water, sometimes straw/hay/manure every 1.5 days. The payoff is not bad but I hate the grind every other day. Wish the capacity in animal pens would be higher so you only have to provide food and water once a week. 
- I recommend use the mods "Seasons" and "Precision Farming". They have some great features to make the game more realistic. Otherwise you can raise every crop everywhere despite of the climate and weather. 
- Graphics look somewhat outdated but there is the new FS 22 coming up by the end of 2021.

You won't get any hint about incompatible mods. So called production mods which for example add factories with non-vanilla goods sometimes result in animal pens not available anymore on a map. I have played every Farming Simulator game since 2009, normally bought on release date. This one is the most discouraging game out the gate.

Pro's
Lighting is vastly improved

Cons
Bugs. Bugs. Bugs. 

Controller support - Before I started the game, I had my joystick hoytas plugged in from another game, plus my controller. I unplugged it, started the game, and the game still wanted to use my hoytas. I had to restart the computer to fix this. Those days were gone when Windows 3.1 came out.

Horses - I guess this is the first attempt, but very derpy controls. Extremely wonky while you are riding. The hitbox is horribly huge, and if you are within what looks like 4 feet of an object, it will block you. You can climb trees with a horse. The idea is solid, but horrible execution.
